sections.heading: Background
sections.wikitext:
The song is a musically upbeat but impassioned plea for [[Toleration|tolerance]] and [[Political freedom|freedom]]:

:''All the world over, so easy to see!''
:''People everywhere, just wanna be free.''
:''Listen, please listen! that's the way it should be''
:''Peace in the valley, people got to be free.''

In the song's coda, Felix says in a half-sung, half-spoken voice, that the "Train of Freedom", is "about to arrive any minute now", that "it has been long, long overdue", and that it's "coming right on through", before the song's fade with Felix saying "Chug" repeatedly.

It became a big hit in the turbulent summer of 1968, spending five weeks atop the [[Billboard Hot 100|US ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart]], the group's longest such stay.<ref>[[Joel Whitburn]], ''The Billboard Book of Top 40 Hits'', Billboard Publications, 1983, p. 223.</ref>  It was also the group's second-most successful single on the [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|''Billboard'' Black Singles chart]], reaching number 14 and trailing only the previous year's "[[Groovin']]".<ref>[{{AllMusic|class=artist|id=p5228/charts-awards/billboard-singles|pure_url=yes}} "The Rascals - Charts and Awards"], [[Allmusic]]. Accessed May 7, 2007.</ref>  "People Got to Be Free" was [[RIAA]]-certified as a [[gold record]] on August 23, 1968,<ref>[https://www.riaa.com/gp/database/default.asp RIAA Searchable Database]</ref> and eventually sold over 4 million copies.<ref>Edward Kiersh, "Felix Cavaliere of The Young Rascals: The Long Winter of Discontent", from ''Where Are You Now, Bo Diddley? The Artists Who Made Us Rock and Where They Are Now'', [[Doubleday (publisher)|Doubleday]], 1986.</ref>  It later was included on the group's March 1969 album ''[[Freedom Suite (The Rascals album)|Freedom Suite]]''. ''Billboard'' ranked the record as the number 5 song for 1968.<ref>[[Billboard Year-End Hot 100 singles of 1968]]</ref>

The single's picture sleeve photo was previously featured in the inner album cover of the Rascals' ''[[Time Peace: The Rascals' Greatest Hits]]'' compilation.  The B-side, "My World", was a track from the group's ''[[Once Upon a Dream (The Rascals album)|Once Upon a Dream]]'' album.

[[Image:The Rascals - PNC 2013 - People Got to Be Free 2.jpg|thumb|right|238px|The Rascals performed "People Got to Be Free" during their 2013 ''Once Upon a Dream'' show, with footage of 1960s civil rights marches displayed on the video screen behind them.]]

While "People Got to Be Free" was perceived by some as related to the [[assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.]] and [[Assassination of Robert F. Kennedy|of Robert F. Kennedy]] earlier that year, it was recorded before the latter's death.  Rather, it was partly a reaction to an ugly encounter wherein the long-haired group was threatened by a group of rednecks, because the group had grown beards and longer hair, after their tour vehicle broke down in [[Fort Pierce, Florida]].<ref>{{cite magazine|last1=Lombardi|first1=John|title=Rascals: The Blackest White Group of All|url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/features/the-blackest-white-group-of-all-19701001|magazine=Rolling Stone|access-date=14 January 2018|date=October 1, 1970}}</ref>

The song is clearly a product of its times; however, two decades later writer [[Dave Marsh]] included it as number 237 in his book ''Heart of Rock and Soul: The 1001 Greatest Singles of All Time'', saying in reference to, and paraphrase of, the song's lyric, "Ask me my opinion, my opinion will be: Dated, but NEVER out of date."

After this song came out, the Rascals would only perform at concerts that featured an African American act; when that condition was not met, the Rascals canceled several shows in protest.

sections.heading: Cover versions
sections.wikitext:
* [[Dionne Warwick]] recorded the song as part of her LP ''[[Soulful (Dionne Warwick album)|Soulful]]'' in 1969, and it was released as a single in the UK in the same year.
* [[The 5th Dimension]] recorded "People Got to Be Free" in 1970 as part of a medley with another socially relevant song, [[Sam Cooke]]'s "[[A Change Is Gonna Come]]." The pairing reached number 60 on the ''Billboard'' Pop Singles chart.<ref>''Joel Whitburn's Top Pop Singles 1955–1990'' - {{ISBN|0-89820-089-X}}</ref>  
* [[Johnny Maestro & the Brooklyn Bridge]] performed this song live in concert, and it has turned up on YouTube as part of The Bridge's "lost tapes" series of songs.
* The Christian group DeGarmo & Key covered this song on their final album, "To Extremes," recorded in 1994.
*The jazz-rock supergroup [[The New York Rock and Soul Revue: Live at the Beacon|The New York Rock and Soul Revue]] covered this song on their 1991 self titled album.
sections.text:
